\chapter{More of the Body}
\label{ch:hi-more-of-the-body}
\hlchaptermodality{53}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five more parts of the body when I say how I am.}

Complete HI-C53-lip and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kandhā]{\hi{कंधा} (kandhā) — a shoulder}

\label{lesson:HI-C53-shoulder}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did the last two words of the chapter before mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{कंधा}}
\textbf{\hi{कंधा}} (\emph{kandhā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a shoulder\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{स्कन्ध} (\emph{skandha}), 'shoulder'. The initial \emph{sk-} cluster could not survive into everyday Hindi and lost its \emph{s}, which is the ordinary fate of a cluster like that in this family.

\emph{Skandha} had a second life meaning 'the trunk of a tree' and then 'a section, a division' — the sense Buddhist texts use for the five aggregates. Hindi kept the shoulder and let the philosophy go.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five more parts of the body.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kandhā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kandhā}, and touch it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{कंधा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a shoulder\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ghuṭnā]{\hi{घुटना} (ghuṭnā) — a knee}

\label{lesson:HI-C53-knee}



\begin{quote}
What did the word before this one mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{घुटना}}
\textbf{\hi{घुटना}} (\emph{ghuṭnā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a knee\textquotedblright{}.

The Sanskrit source is \hi{घुण्ट} (\emph{ghuṇṭa}), a word for the ankle or knee joint, though the details of how it arrived are not agreed on.

Be careful with this one in a dictionary: \hi{घुटना} is also a verb meaning 'to be stifled', and the two are unrelated. Hindi has a small number of these exact collisions, and the only way through is the sentence around the word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The second of five, and a word with a twin that means something else entirely.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ghuṭnā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ghuṭnā}, then \emph{kandhā} — the joint low, the joint high
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{घुटना} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a knee\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[māthā]{\hi{माथा} (māthā) — a forehead}

\label{lesson:HI-C53-forehead}



\begin{quote}
Name the 2 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{माथा}}
\textbf{\hi{माथा}} (\emph{māthā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a forehead\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{मस्तक} (\emph{mastaka}), 'head'. The everyday word narrowed as it wore down: what meant the whole head now means the front of it.

\hi{मस्तक} itself is still in Hindi, unworn, in formal and literary registers. So you have another register doublet of the kind you met with \hi{सुबह} beside \hi{प्रभात} — the same ancestor arriving twice, once eroded and everyday, once intact and bookish.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The third of five, and a narrowing you can watch happen.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{māthā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{māthā}, and then \hi{सिर}, which you met when the head was first named
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{माथा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a forehead\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pīṭh]{\hi{पीठ} (pīṭh) — the back}

\label{lesson:HI-C53-back}



\begin{quote}
Name the 3 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{पीठ}}
\textbf{\hi{पीठ}} (\emph{pīṭh}) — \textquotedblleft{}the back\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{पृष्ठ} (\emph{pṛṣṭha}), 'back, surface'. The heavy \emph{-ṛṣṭh-} in the middle collapsed and paid for itself by lengthening the vowel in front of it.

That is the same bargain that gave you \hi{कान} out of \emph{karṇa} when the ear was named — a cluster gives way, and the vowel before it grows to keep the syllable's weight. Once you have seen the trade twice it stops looking like an exception.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fourth of five, and the second time you have seen that trade.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pīṭh}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{pīṭh}, then \emph{kandhā} — the back and the shoulder above it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{पीठ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the back\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hoṇṭh]{\hi{होंठ} (hoṇṭh) — a lip}

\label{lesson:HI-C53-lip}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{होंठ}}
\textbf{\hi{होंठ}} (\emph{hoṇṭh}) — \textquotedblleft{}a lip\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{ओष्ठ} (\emph{oṣṭha}), 'lip'. Hindi added the nasal in the middle and an \emph{h} at the front, both of which are ordinary enough in this line of descent.

Do not reach for Latin \emph{labium} as a cousin here — it is not one. Two Indo-European languages can have perfectly ordinary words for the same body part that descend from completely different roots, which you have already met with \hi{रात} beside \emph{nox}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fifth of five. That is the body, from the forehead down.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hoṇṭh}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{hoṇṭh}, \emph{māthā}, \emph{kandhā}, \emph{pīṭh}, \emph{ghuṭnā} — top to bottom
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{होंठ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a lip\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
